title: Know Your Worth
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Anchored around the well-known Picasso napkin anecdote, this article makes the case that expertise should be valued for the years of accumulated skill behind it, not the minutes it takes to apply. When an admirer balked at Picasso's fee for a three-minute sketch, the artist's reply, "it took me all my life," becomes the piece's central argument for how experts should think about their own compensation. The author extends this beyond famous examples like lawyers, surgeons, and athletes, urging any reader with real competence not to underestimate its value just because true expertise is rarer than people assume. It closes with a blunt directive: charge for what a lifetime of developed skill is actually worth.
points: The Picasso napkin story illustrates that expertise should be priced by the years behind the skill, not the minutes it takes to execute.
High-value expertise, legal, medical, creative, athletic, commands premium pricing precisely because it's built over a lifetime, not overnight.
The article argues genuine competence is rarer than most people assume, which is a reason not to underprice one's own skill or time.
The closing directive frames self-advocacy about compensation as a natural extension of respecting one's own accumulated expertise.
quotes: The value of expertise is uneven and hard to measure. Those with the experience, know-how, street smarts, and acumen to apply their knowledge to important problems and opportunities will always be in high demand.
As the story goes, the legendary artist Pablo Picasso was at a Paris restaurant when an admirer approached him and asked if he could do a quick sketch on a paper napkin.
The patron exclaimed, “40,000 francs! It only took you three minutes.” Picasso coolly replied, “No, it took me all my life.
Competence is not as common as people think. Truly competent people are unusually rare.
They ask and expect a reward equal to their merit. It took you all your life to get here. Charge for it.
